title: Rivet and Daillé citations: dispute heat can force soft readings; they would not desert Ames/British sense
source_text: CXL. Frustra vero vir Doctus objicit testimonia virorum, qui sunt multum inter Reformatos celebres, Andreae Riveti, & Joannis Dallaéi; quos ex quibusdam eorum verbis probare conatur, eandem certitudinem tribuisse fiduciae, quam quis habet de gratia & salute propria, quae convenit eorum judicio fidei, quae adhibenda est ipsis fundamentalibus fidei articulis. Sed certe notum omnibus est, viris etiam doctissimis, dum disputationis aestu abripiuntur, incaute multa excidere, quae emollire & torquere quodammodo opus est, ut ad bonum sensum reducantur; nec dubito viros illos Doctos, si hac de re moniti fuissent, mentem suam fuisse declaraturos ea ratione, ut ab exposita jam sententia non discessissent.
pass_a_gloss: In vain truly does the Learned Man object the testimonies of men who are much celebrated among the Reformed, Andrew Rivet and Jean Daillé; whom from certain of their words he tries to prove to have attributed to the fiducia which someone has concerning his own grace and salvation the same certainty which, in their judgment, belongs to the faith that must be applied to the fundamental articles of faith themselves. But certainly it is known to all that even to the most learned men, when they are carried away by the heat of disputation, many things escape uncautiously which it is necessary somehow to soften and twist so that they may be brought back to a good sense; nor do I doubt that those Learned men, if they had been admonished on this matter, would have declared their mind in such a way that they would not have departed from the sentence already set forth.
pass_b_english: The opponent's Rivet and Daillé citations fail: from a few words he claims they gave own-grace fiducia the same certainty as faith in the fundamentals.
Even the most learned, caught in dispute heat, let slip things that need softening back to a sound sense.
Le Blanc doubts that, if warned, those doctors would have left the Ames/British sentence already laid out.
